rows.stem:
Answer the following questions (Do any two) :
(a) Identify the order of reaction from the following unit for its rate constant :
\(\mathrm{Lmol^{-1}s^{-1}}\)
(b) The conversion of molecules A to B follow second order kinetics. If concentration of A is increased to three times, how will it affect the rate of formation of B?
(c) Write the expression of integrated rate equation for zero order reaction.
rows.solution:
(a) The order is SECOND.

For a reaction of order \(n\) the rate constant carries the units
\(k = \dfrac{\text{Rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^n}\), that is \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

Matching the given \(\mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\): the exponent of litre is \(n - 1 = 1\), so \(n = 2\), and the exponent of mole is \(1 - n = -1\), which agrees.

The short list is worth remembering: zero order \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\), first order \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), second order \(\mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

(b) The rate becomes NINE TIMES its original value.

Second order in A means \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^2\), so tripling the concentration multiplies the rate by \(3^2 = 9\).

(c) The INTEGRATED RATE EQUATION for a zero order reaction is
\([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\), or equivalently \(k = \dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0 - [\mathrm{R}]}{t}\)

A zero order reaction proceeds at a CONSTANT rate whatever the concentration, so the concentration falls LINEARLY with time — a plot of \([\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\) is a straight line of slope \(-k\).

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Arrange the following in the increasing order of their property indicated :
(a) Ethanal, Propanone, Propanal, Butanone (reactivity towards nucleophilic addition)
(b) 4-Nitrobenzoic acid, benzoic acid, 3,4-Dinitrobenzoic acid, 4-Methoxy benzoic acid (Acid strength)
rows.solution:
(a) Increasing reactivity towards nucleophilic addition:
BUTANONE < PROPANONE < PROPANAL < ETHANAL

Nucleophilic addition begins with a nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon, so reactivity falls as that carbon is made less positive and more crowded — and every ALKYL group does both, releasing electron density inductively and blocking the approach.

The two KETONES come first, each with two alkyl groups, and butanone is the more hindered of them, its ethyl group bulkier than a methyl. The two ALDEHYDES follow with one alkyl group each, and ethanal outranks propanal for the same reason.

(b) Increasing acid strength:
4-METHOXYBENZOIC ACID < BENZOIC ACID < 4-NITROBENZOIC ACID < 3,4-DINITROBENZOIC ACID

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the carboxylate anion, and a ring substituent acts through both induction and resonance.

The METHOXY group DONATES a lone pair into the ring, raising the electron density, intensifying the charge on the anion and WEAKENING the acid. The NITRO group WITHDRAWS, stabilising the anion and STRENGTHENING it. TWO nitro groups withdraw more than one, so the dinitro acid is strongest of all.

Benzoic acid, with neither substituent, sits between the methoxy and the nitro compounds.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Explain the following reactions :
(a) Wolff Kishner reduction
(b) Cannizzaro reaction
rows.solution:
(a) WOLFF-KISHNER REDUCTION converts the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone all the way to a \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group, in two stages.

First hydrazine condenses with the carbonyl, losing water to give the HYDRAZONE. Then heating that with a strong base in a high-boiling solvent expels nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}} \mathrm{C{=}N{-}NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{KOH}/\text{ethylene glycol}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

The nitrogen leaving as a gas is what drives the reaction. The conditions are ALKALINE, which is the practical difference from the Clemmensen reduction — that achieves the same conversion with zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid, and the choice between them depends on whether the rest of the molecule can survive acid or base.

(b) CANNIZZARO'S REACTION is a DISPROPORTIONATION of an aldehyde having NO \(\alpha\) HYDROGEN, treated with concentrated alkali. One molecule is OXIDISED to the salt of an acid while another is REDUCED to an alcohol:
\(2\,\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{NaOH\ (conc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HCOONa}\)

Benzaldehyde behaves the same way, giving benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate.

The absence of an \(\alpha\) hydrogen is what makes this route available: an aldehyde that HAS one forms an enolate instead and undergoes the aldol condensation.

rows.stem:
Observe the graph shown in figure and answer the following questions :
(a) What is the order of the reaction ?
(b) What is the slope of the curve?
(c) Write the relationship between \(k\) and \(t_{1/2}\) (half life period)
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the whole question is 'observe the graph shown in figure'; the stem names no data at all and the printed plot is the only source of it. The plot is DELIBERATELY NOT described here, because reading its axes IS the answer to sub-part (a). Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The graph plots \(\log\left([\mathrm{R}]_0/[\mathrm{R}]\right)\) against TIME and gives a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN.

(a) The reaction is FIRST ORDER.

The integrated first order rate law rearranges to exactly the form the graph shows:
\(\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\,t\)

A straight line through the origin is what that equation predicts, and no other order gives one — a zero order reaction gives a straight line for \([\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\), and a second order one for \(1/[\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\).

(b) The SLOPE is \(\dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\).

Comparing with \(y = mx\), the coefficient of \(t\) is the slope. So measuring the slope of such a plot is the standard way of finding the rate constant: \(k = 2{\cdot}303 \times \text{slope}\).

(c) The relationship between the rate constant and the half-life is
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\)

Note what is absent from it: the INITIAL CONCENTRATION. For a first order reaction the half-life is entirely independent of how much material one starts with, which is why radioactive decay has a fixed half-life whatever the size of the sample.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the IUPAC name of the following complex :
\(\mathrm{K_2[PdCl_4]}\)
(ii) Using crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{d^5}\) ion, if \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\).
(iii) What are Homoleptic complexes?
rows.solution:
(i) The complex is the ANION — two potassiums outside make it \(2-\) — so its name takes the \(-\mathrm{ATE}\) suffix. Four chlorido ligands give \(-4\) against that \(2-\), so palladium is \(+2\):
POTASSIUM TETRACHLORIDOPALLADATE(II)

The cation is named first and written as a separate word, exactly as in an ordinary salt.

(ii) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^5\,e_g^0\).

An octahedral field splits the d orbitals into a lower set of three and an upper set of two, separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron chooses between promotion to the upper set, costing \(\Delta_0\), and pairing in the lower set, costing the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

With \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\) — a STRONG FIELD — pairing is cheaper, so all five electrons crowd into the three lower orbitals as two pairs and one single. This is a LOW SPIN complex with ONE unpaired electron, \(\mu = 1{\cdot}73\) B.M.

(iii) A HOMOLEPTIC complex is one in which the metal is bound to only ONE KIND of donor group — every ligand is the same.

Examples: \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\), where all six ligands are ammonia, and \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\).

The contrast is a HETEROLEPTIC complex, bound to more than one kind of ligand — \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^+}\), for instance. Only a heteroleptic complex can show geometrical isomerism, since there must be different ligands for their arrangement to differ.

rows.stem:
(i) Why chelate complexes are more stable than complexes with unidentate ligands ?
(ii) What is "spectrochemical series" ? What is the difference between a weak field ligand and a strong field ligand ?
rows.solution:
(i) Because of the CHELATE EFFECT.

A chelating ligand is POLYDENTATE: it binds the metal through two or more donor atoms at once, closing a RING that includes the metal. Ethylenediamine closes a five-membered ring; oxalate does the same; a unidentate ligand such as ammonia closes none.

Two reasons make the chelate the more stable. Once one donor atom has attached, the second is held CLOSE to the metal by the ligand's own framework and binds readily, whereas a separate ligand would have to arrive from solution. And releasing a chelating ligand requires TWO bonds to break AT ONCE rather than one, which is far less likely.

There is also a thermodynamic way of putting it: three bidentate ligands replacing six unidentate ones increase the number of free particles in solution, so the ENTROPY rises and the reaction is favoured.

(ii) The SPECTROCHEMICAL SERIES is the arrangement of ligands in order of the CRYSTAL FIELD SPLITTING ENERGY they produce for a given metal ion:
\(\mathrm{I^-} < \mathrm{Br^-} < \mathrm{Cl^-} < \mathrm{F^-} < \mathrm{OH^-} < \mathrm{H_2O} < \mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{en} < \mathrm{NO_2^-} < \mathrm{CN^-} < \mathrm{CO}\)

It is an EXPERIMENTAL order, established from the absorption spectra of the complexes — hence the name.

A WEAK FIELD LIGAND produces a SMALL \(\Delta_0\), smaller than the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\). The electrons then prefer to occupy the upper orbitals singly rather than pair up, giving a HIGH SPIN complex with the maximum number of unpaired electrons. The halides and water are weak field ligands.

A STRONG FIELD LIGAND produces a LARGE \(\Delta_0\), greater than \(\mathrm{P}\). Pairing is then the cheaper option, so the lower set fills completely before any electron reaches the upper, giving a LOW SPIN complex. Cyanide and carbon monoxide are the strongest.

rows.stem:
(i) Define coagulation.
(ii) State Hardy-Schulze rule.
(iii) What is Electrophoresis?
rows.solution:
(i) COAGULATION is the settling of colloidal particles — the conversion of a colloidal SOL into a PRECIPITATE.

It happens when the CHARGE on the particles is neutralised so that they can no longer repel one another; they then collide, grow heavy enough to overcome Brownian movement, and fall out. Adding an electrolyte is the usual way, but boiling, persistent dialysis and mixing two oppositely charged sols all do it.

(ii) HARDY-SCHULZE RULE states that the coagulating power of an ion increases with its VALENCY — and it is the ion carrying the charge OPPOSITE to that of the sol particles that does the coagulating.

So for a NEGATIVE sol such as arsenic(III) sulphide the coagulating power of the cations runs \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}} > \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} > \mathrm{Na^+}\); for a POSITIVE sol such as iron(III) hydroxide it is the anions that matter, \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}} > \mathrm{PO_4^{3-}} > \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} > \mathrm{Cl^-}\).

The rule explains why the Ganges forms a delta: the river's colloidal clay is coagulated by the ions of sea water.

(iii) ELECTROPHORESIS is the MOVEMENT OF COLLOIDAL PARTICLES towards one electrode under an applied electric field.

Because the particles carry a charge, they migrate — a positive sol towards the cathode, a negative sol towards the anode — and their eventual discharge at the electrode coagulates them.

The direction of movement therefore REVEALS the sign of the charge, and the process is used industrially to remove smoke from factory chimneys in the Cottrell precipitator.

rows.stem: Write three differences between Physisorption and Chemisorption.
rows.solution:
Three differences between physisorption and chemisorption.

NATURE OF THE FORCES. PHYSISORPTION arises from weak VAN DER WAALS forces between the adsorbate and the surface. CHEMISORPTION involves genuine CHEMICAL BONDS, a surface compound effectively forming.

REVERSIBILITY. Physisorption is REVERSIBLE — the weak forces are easily overcome, so lowering the pressure or raising the temperature releases the gas. Chemisorption is essentially IRREVERSIBLE.

NUMBER OF LAYERS. Physisorption forms MULTIMOLECULAR layers, a physisorbed layer being able to attract further molecules on top of it. Chemisorption forms a UNIMOLECULAR layer only, because once every surface site has formed its bond there is nothing left to bond to.

Two further contrasts follow from the same difference in bond strength: the enthalpy of adsorption is small for physisorption, about 20 to 40 kJ per mole, and large for chemisorption, 80 to 240; and physisorption is NOT SPECIFIC, any gas adsorbing on any solid, whereas chemisorption is HIGHLY SPECIFIC, occurring only where a bond can actually form.

rows.stem:
(a) Write any two consequences of Lanthanoid Contraction.
(b) Name the element of 3d series which exhibits the largest number of oxidation states. Give reason.
rows.solution:
(a) TWO CONSEQUENCES of the lanthanoid contraction.

ZIRCONIUM AND HAFNIUM HAVE ALMOST IDENTICAL RADII, about 160 pm each, although hafnium lies a whole period lower. The fourteen lanthanoids intervening between them cancel the increase expected from the extra period, so the two elements behave so alike that they occur together in nature and are notoriously difficult to separate.

THE LANTHANOIDS THEMSELVES ARE DIFFICULT TO SEPARATE, being so close in size and almost all in the \(+3\) state — so ion-exchange or solvent extraction, exploiting minute differences, must be used instead of ordinary chemical methods.

A third consequence: the BASIC CHARACTER of the hydroxides falls steadily from \(\mathrm{La(OH)_3}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu(OH)_3}\), as the shrinking ion holds the hydroxide more tightly.

(b) MANGANESE exhibits the largest number of oxidation states — every one from \(+2\) to \(+7\).

The reason lies in its electron count. Manganese is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\), so it has FIVE UNPAIRED \(3d\) electrons plus TWO \(4s\) electrons. All seven lie close in energy and are available for bonding, and no other element of the series has as many available at once.

From iron onwards the \(3d\) electrons begin to PAIR UP, and a paired electron is less readily used for bonding — which is why the range of states narrows again after manganese.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following statements :
(a) Copper does not displace hydrogen from acids.
(b) Transition metals and most of their compounds show paramagnetic behaviour.
(c) Zn, Cd and Hg are soft metals.
rows.solution:
(a) Because copper's \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}}\) is POSITIVE, at \(+0{\cdot}34\) V — the only such value in the 3d series.

Displacing hydrogen requires a metal to be oxidised more readily than hydrogen, which means a NEGATIVE reduction potential. Copper's is positive, so it cannot.

Why it is positive: converting the solid metal to hydrated \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) takes three steps, and the energy recovered in the last must pay for the first two. Copper has a HIGH enthalpy of atomisation and its ionisation energies are large, while its HYDRATION enthalpy is not large enough to cover them. The books do not balance.

Nitric acid does dissolve copper, but by OXIDISING it rather than by displacing hydrogen — which is why nitrogen oxides are evolved instead of hydrogen.

(b) Because they have UNPAIRED d ELECTRONS.

Paramagnetism is the property of being attracted into a magnetic field, and it requires unpaired electrons — each behaves as a tiny magnet, and in the absence of a partner of opposite spin its moment is not cancelled.

A transition metal has a partly filled d subshell almost by definition, so unpaired electrons are the rule rather than the exception. The magnetic moment measures how many:
\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \mathrm{B.M.}\)

The exceptions prove the point: \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(d^0\) and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(d^{10}\), and both are DIAMAGNETIC.

(c) Because their d subshells are COMPLETELY FILLED, so their d electrons take no part in metallic bonding.

The hardness of a metal reflects the strength of the bond holding its lattice together, and in a transition metal the UNPAIRED d electrons contribute to that bond alongside the \(s\) electrons. Zinc, cadmium and mercury are \(d^{10}\): every d electron is paired and held tightly to its own atom, so only the two \(s\) electrons are available.

The metallic bond is correspondingly weak, and the metals are soft with low melting points — mercury being liquid at room temperature.

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{pk_b}\) of aniline is more than that of methylamine.
(ii) Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
(iii) Primary amines have higher boiling points than tertiary amines.
rows.solution:
(i) Because aniline's lone pair is DELOCALISED into the benzene ring.

A higher \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a WEAKER base, and a base is weak when its lone pair is not available to accept a proton.

In aniline the nitrogen is attached directly to the ring, so its lone pair is spread over the ortho and para carbons by resonance and is much less available. In methylamine the nitrogen's lone pair stays on the nitrogen, and the methyl group even pushes further density onto it.

The gap is large: \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) 9.38 for aniline against 3.38 for methylamine, about \(10^6\) in base strength.

(ii) Because the amino group reacts with the CATALYST.

A Friedel-Crafts reaction needs anhydrous aluminium chloride, a LEWIS ACID, and aniline's nitrogen lone pair makes it a Lewis BASE — so the two combine at once to form a salt. The catalyst is consumed, and the nitrogen now carries a POSITIVE charge which strongly DEACTIVATES the ring, so no electrophilic substitution occurs.

(iii) Because primary amines can form HYDROGEN BONDS with one another and tertiary amines cannot.

A hydrogen bond needs a hydrogen attached to nitrogen. A PRIMARY amine has TWO such hydrogens, so its molecules associate extensively and a great deal of energy is needed to separate them. A SECONDARY amine has one. A TERTIARY amine has NONE — its nitrogen carries three alkyl groups — so its molecules attract one another only by weak dipole-dipole forces.

Among amines of comparable molar mass the boiling points therefore run primary > secondary > tertiary.

rows.stem:
(i) Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their basic strength in aqueous solution :
\(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\)
(ii) What is Hinsberg's reagent ?
(iii) What is the role of pyridine in the acylation reaction of amines?
rows.solution:
(i) Increasing basic strength in aqueous solution:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N} < \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} < (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH}\)

Two effects compete in water and neither wins outright. Each methyl group RELEASES electron density and makes the lone pair more available, which favours the tertiary amine. But the conjugate acid must be STABILISED BY HYDROGEN BONDING to water, which needs hydrogens on the nitrogen — three for the primary amine's cation, two for the secondary, only one for the tertiary — and three bulky methyl groups also obstruct a proton's approach.

The SECONDARY amine, sharing in both advantages, comes out strongest; the tertiary, penalised twice, comes out weakest. In the GAS PHASE, where no solvent can hydrogen bond, the order is purely inductive and trimethylamine is the strongest.

(ii) HINSBERG'S REAGENT is BENZENESULPHONYL CHLORIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\).

It distinguishes the three classes of amine. A PRIMARY amine gives a sulphonamide that still carries a hydrogen on its nitrogen, made acidic by the two sulphonyl oxygens, so the product DISSOLVES in alkali. A SECONDARY amine gives one with no such hydrogen, INSOLUBLE in alkali. A TERTIARY amine, having no \(\mathrm{N-H}\) at all, does not react.

(iii) PYRIDINE acts as a BASE, and its role is twofold.

Acylation liberates HYDROGEN CHLORIDE, and pyridine absorbs it. That shifts the equilibrium FORWARD, towards the amide.

More importantly, it protects the AMINE. Without pyridine the hydrogen chloride would protonate the amine, converting it to its salt — and a protonated amine has no lone pair left, so it is no longer nucleophilic and the reaction would stop after half the amine had been consumed.

rows.stem: A compound 'A' on reduction with iron scrap and hydrochloric acid gives compound 'B' with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_7N}\). Compound 'B' on reaction with \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) and alcoholic KOH produces an obnoxious smell of carbylamine due to the formation of 'C'. Identify 'A', 'B' and 'C' and write the chemical reactions involved.
rows.solution:
Compound 'B' has the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_6H_7N}\) and gives the CARBYLAMINE reaction, so it is a PRIMARY amine with a benzene ring:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

It is obtained by REDUCTION with iron scrap and hydrochloric acid, and what such a reduction converts into an amino group is a NITRO group:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2}\), nitrobenzene
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} + 6[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The obnoxious smell is the isocyanide:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NC}\), phenyl isocyanide
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The carbylamine reaction is a test for PRIMARY amines alone, because forming the isocyanide requires the nitrogen to give up BOTH of its hydrogens — so the smell also confirms the identification of 'B'.

rows.stem:
Complete the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3CN}\) \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{2.\ H_2O}]{\mathrm{1.\ A1H(i\text{-}Bu)_2}}\) 'A' \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^{+}}]{\mathrm{H_2N\text{-}OH}}\) 'B'
(ii) Write IUPAC name of the following compound:
(iii) Write chemical test to distinguish between the following compounds :
Phenol and Benzoic acid
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — sub-part (ii) prints its compound ONLY as a drawing and asks for its IUPAC name, so the row is unanswerable from text alone. Described here rather than named, because naming it would state the answer: a hexagonal benzene ring, a -CHO group bonded to its upper-right vertex, and a Br substituent on the ring two positions round from that vertex. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
(i) DIBAL-H — diisobutylaluminium hydride — is a mild reducing agent that stops a nitrile at the IMINE stage, which water then hydrolyses:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), ethanal

Hydroxylamine then condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}N{-}OH}\), ethanal oxime

The point of DIBAL-H is that it STOPS at the aldehyde; lithium aluminium hydride would carry the reduction on to the primary amine, and no oxime would be possible.

(ii) 3-BROMOBENZALDEHYDE, also written 3-bromobenzenecarbaldehyde.

The \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group takes position 1 as the principal characteristic group, and the bromine sits at the META position.

(iii) Add SODIUM HYDROGENCARBONATE solution to each. BENZOIC ACID gives brisk EFFERVESCENCE of carbon dioxide; PHENOL gives none:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} + \mathrm{NaHCO_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow\)

The test discriminates because of a difference in ACID STRENGTH. Benzoic acid, \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 4.19, is stronger than carbonic acid and displaces carbon dioxide from its salt. Phenol, \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 10.0, is much weaker than carbonic acid and cannot — although it IS acidic enough to dissolve in sodium hydroxide, which is why that reagent would NOT distinguish them.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Convert the following :
(i) Benzoic acid to Benzaldehyde
(ii) Propan-1-ol to 2-Bromopropanoic acid
(iii) Acetaldehyde to But-2-enal
rows.solution:
(i) BENZOIC ACID TO BENZALDEHYDE, in two steps. An acid cannot be reduced directly to an aldehyde without going past it, so it is first converted to the ACYL CHLORIDE:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2}/\mathrm{Pd\text{-}BaSO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)

The second step is ROSENMUND'S REDUCTION, whose deliberately POISONED catalyst is what stops the reduction at the aldehyde rather than carrying it on to benzyl alcohol.

(ii) PROPAN-1-OL TO 2-BROMOPROPANOIC ACID, in two stages. First oxidise the primary alcohol all the way to the acid, then halogenate at the \(\alpha\) position:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \text{alk. }\mathrm{KMnO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \mathrm{Br_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)COOH}\)

The second step is the HELL-VOLHARD-ZELINSKY reaction, and the red phosphorus is essential: it converts the acid into its acyl bromide, which enolises far more readily, and it is the enol that bromine attacks.

(iii) ACETALDEHYDE TO BUT-2-ENAL — count the carbons: TWO in, FOUR out, so two molecules must be joined. This is the ALDOL CONDENSATION:
\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH{-}CHO} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The HEATING is what carries it past the aldol: the new double bond is conjugated with the carbonyl, and that stability drives the loss of water.

rows.stem: Is silver plate the anode or cathode?
rows.context:
Oxidation-reduction reactions are commonly known as redox reactions. They involve transfer of electrons from one species to another. In a spontaneous reaction, energy is released which can be used to do useful work. The reaction is split into two half reactions. Two different containers are used and a wire is used to drive the electrons from one side to the other and a Voltaic/Galvanic cell is created. It is an electrochemical cell that uses spontaneous redox reactions to generate electricity. A salt bridge also connects to the half cells. The reading of the voltmeter gives the cell voltage or cell potential or electromotive force. If \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) is positive the reaction is spontaneous and if it is negative the reaction is non-spontaneous and is referred to as electrolytic cell. Electrolysis refers to the decomposition of a substance by an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
The conductance of material is the property of materials due to which a material allows the flow of ions through itself and thus conducts electricity. Conductivity is represented by k and it depends upon nature and concentration of electrolyte, temperature etc. A more common term molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is conductance of the volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with the unit area of cross-section and distance of unit length. Limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes cannot be obtained graphically.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — 'silver plate' appears NOWHERE in the passage; it is a label on the drawn cell, so without the figure the stem names a referent the reader has never met. The drawing shows two beakers, I on the left with a zinc plate in a \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)}\) solution and II on the right with a silver plate in \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)}\), joined by a salt bridge and by an external wire through a voltmeter. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The SILVER plate is the CATHODE.

In a galvanic cell the CATHODE is where REDUCTION happens, and the half cell with the HIGHER reduction potential takes that role. Silver's \(E^{\circ}\) is \(+0{\cdot}80\) V against zinc's \(-0{\cdot}76\) V, so silver ions are reduced and deposited on the plate while zinc metal dissolves:
at the cathode, \(\mathrm{Ag^+} + e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}\)
at the anode, \(\mathrm{Zn} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2e^-\)

Note that in a GALVANIC cell the cathode is the POSITIVE terminal, the reverse of an electrolytic cell — the sign follows from the direction the electrons flow, not from the name.

rows.stem: What will happen if the salt bridge is removed?
rows.context:
Oxidation-reduction reactions are commonly known as redox reactions. They involve transfer of electrons from one species to another. In a spontaneous reaction, energy is released which can be used to do useful work. The reaction is split into two half reactions. Two different containers are used and a wire is used to drive the electrons from one side to the other and a Voltaic/Galvanic cell is created. It is an electrochemical cell that uses spontaneous redox reactions to generate electricity. A salt bridge also connects to the half cells. The reading of the voltmeter gives the cell voltage or cell potential or electromotive force. If \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) is positive the reaction is spontaneous and if it is negative the reaction is non-spontaneous and is referred to as electrolytic cell. Electrolysis refers to the decomposition of a substance by an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
The conductance of material is the property of materials due to which a material allows the flow of ions through itself and thus conducts electricity. Conductivity is represented by k and it depends upon nature and concentration of electrolyte, temperature etc. A more common term molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is conductance of the volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with the unit area of cross-section and distance of unit length. Limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes cannot be obtained graphically.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — 'the salt bridge' is definite and points at the one drawn between beakers I and II; the passage mentions a salt bridge only in the abstract. This stem is also generic enough to be reprinted verbatim in a sibling set over a DIFFERENT cell, which is exactly the hash-collision case REQUIRED guards against. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The CELL STOPS WORKING — no current flows and the voltmeter reading falls to zero.

The salt bridge does a job the wire cannot. As the cell runs, the anode compartment accumulates \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) and so a POSITIVE charge, while the cathode compartment loses \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) and so becomes NEGATIVE. The salt bridge supplies ions to both — anions to the anode side and cations to the cathode side — and so keeps each solution electrically NEUTRAL.

Remove it and that build-up of charge is unopposed. It immediately opposes any further transfer of electrons, so the reaction halts almost as soon as it begins.

The salt bridge also COMPLETES the circuit, carrying the current through the solution between the two beakers, and it prevents the two solutions from mixing directly.

rows.stem: When does electrochemical cell behaves like an electrolytic cell?
rows.context:
Oxidation-reduction reactions are commonly known as redox reactions. They involve transfer of electrons from one species to another. In a spontaneous reaction, energy is released which can be used to do useful work. The reaction is split into two half reactions. Two different containers are used and a wire is used to drive the electrons from one side to the other and a Voltaic/Galvanic cell is created. It is an electrochemical cell that uses spontaneous redox reactions to generate electricity. A salt bridge also connects to the half cells. The reading of the voltmeter gives the cell voltage or cell potential or electromotive force. If \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) is positive the reaction is spontaneous and if it is negative the reaction is non-spontaneous and is referred to as electrolytic cell. Electrolysis refers to the decomposition of a substance by an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
The conductance of material is the property of materials due to which a material allows the flow of ions through itself and thus conducts electricity. Conductivity is represented by k and it depends upon nature and concentration of electrolyte, temperature etc. A more common term molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is conductance of the volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with the unit area of cross-section and distance of unit length. Limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes cannot be obtained graphically.
rows.solution:
An electrochemical cell behaves like an ELECTROLYTIC cell when the EXTERNAL potential applied to it EXCEEDS its own cell potential:
\(E_{\text{external}} > E_{\text{cell}}\)

Below that point the cell drives current in its own direction and the spontaneous reaction proceeds. When the two are exactly EQUAL no current flows at all and the reaction stops — the null point used in measuring emf.

Once the external potential is the greater, current is forced through in the OPPOSITE direction and every electrode reaction runs BACKWARDS. The cell is now consuming electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction, which is what an electrolytic cell does.

This is exactly what happens when a lead storage battery is recharged.

rows.stem:
(i) What will happen to the concentration of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) when \(\mathrm{E_{cell}} = 0\).
(ii) Why does conductivity of a solution decreases with dilution?
rows.context:
Oxidation-reduction reactions are commonly known as redox reactions. They involve transfer of electrons from one species to another. In a spontaneous reaction, energy is released which can be used to do useful work. The reaction is split into two half reactions. Two different containers are used and a wire is used to drive the electrons from one side to the other and a Voltaic/Galvanic cell is created. It is an electrochemical cell that uses spontaneous redox reactions to generate electricity. A salt bridge also connects to the half cells. The reading of the voltmeter gives the cell voltage or cell potential or electromotive force. If \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) is positive the reaction is spontaneous and if it is negative the reaction is non-spontaneous and is referred to as electrolytic cell. Electrolysis refers to the decomposition of a substance by an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
The conductance of material is the property of materials due to which a material allows the flow of ions through itself and thus conducts electricity. Conductivity is represented by k and it depends upon nature and concentration of electrolyte, temperature etc. A more common term molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is conductance of the volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with the unit area of cross-section and distance of unit length. Limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes cannot be obtained graphically.
rows.solution:
(i) Their concentrations will NOT CHANGE any further — the cell has reached EQUILIBRIUM.

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\) means the cell can do no more work. The forward and backward reactions are now proceeding at equal rates, so zinc is dissolving and depositing at the same rate and silver likewise. The concentrations have settled at whatever values satisfy
\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{n}\log \mathrm{K_C}\)

and they stay there. The cell is exhausted — "dead" — although the chemicals are still present.

(ii) Because the number of IONS PER UNIT VOLUME decreases.

Conductivity is the conductance of a FIXED VOLUME of solution — the block held between electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre. What carries the current through it is the ions inside, so the conductivity depends on how many there are per unit volume.

Diluting spreads the same ions through more solution, so that fixed block holds fewer of them and conducts less.

MOLAR conductivity behaves the OPPOSITE way and rises on dilution, because it counts the conductance furnished by a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte rather than a fixed volume.

rows.stem: The molar conductivity of a 1.5 M solution of an electrolyte is found to be 138.9 S \(\mathrm{cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\). Calculate the conductivity of this solution.
rows.context:
Oxidation-reduction reactions are commonly known as redox reactions. They involve transfer of electrons from one species to another. In a spontaneous reaction, energy is released which can be used to do useful work. The reaction is split into two half reactions. Two different containers are used and a wire is used to drive the electrons from one side to the other and a Voltaic/Galvanic cell is created. It is an electrochemical cell that uses spontaneous redox reactions to generate electricity. A salt bridge also connects to the half cells. The reading of the voltmeter gives the cell voltage or cell potential or electromotive force. If \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) is positive the reaction is spontaneous and if it is negative the reaction is non-spontaneous and is referred to as electrolytic cell. Electrolysis refers to the decomposition of a substance by an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
The conductance of material is the property of materials due to which a material allows the flow of ions through itself and thus conducts electricity. Conductivity is represented by k and it depends upon nature and concentration of electrolyte, temperature etc. A more common term molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is conductance of the volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with the unit area of cross-section and distance of unit length. Limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes cannot be obtained graphically.
rows.solution:
Rearrange the definition of molar conductivity to give the conductivity:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{\mathrm{C}}\), so \(\kappa = \dfrac{\Lambda_m \times \mathrm{C}}{1000}\)

Substituting the values given:
\(\kappa = \dfrac{138{\cdot}9 \times 1{\cdot}5}{1000} = \dfrac{208{\cdot}35}{1000}\)

\(\kappa = 0{\cdot}208\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

The factor of 1000 is what the question tests. It converts litres to cubic centimetres: \(\kappa\) is quoted per CENTIMETRE while the concentration is per LITRE, and without the conversion the answer would be out by a thousand.

The magnitude is a check in itself — a conductivity of a fraction of a siemens per centimetre is what a reasonably concentrated electrolyte gives, while 208 would be impossibly large.
